dehydrated_text:
I see deeply within myself not needing my eyes; I can see everything clearly. Why would I want to bother with my physical eyes when I perceive the world through his eyes—through Asha's, through the Monad, and through our master? That’s how you should see: through your imagination. You can imagine a better world, and if you do, you can create it.

Don't be fooled by the material world; it is all an illusion—not Christian or Jew or Muslim, not Hindu, Buddhist, Sufi, or Zen. I am neither from the east nor the west, not out of the ocean or up from the ground; I am not natural or ether; I do not exist as a separate entity in this world or the next. My place is placeless, a trace of the traceless—neither body nor soul. We are all part of God; that’s our true nature.

There's a divine spark within us. Don't be fooled by labels; Christians, Buddhists, Jews—all are children of God. So don't let labels deceive you. There's a joke: God and Satan are fighting over humanity. God says humans have discovered religion, so I've won. But Satan retorts, "Then I'll organize it." The idea is that religion is great, but organized religion serves the interests of priests who control it.

Judaism, Islam, Christianity—differences exist because those in charge need to differentiate and exploit you to justify their existence. At the end of the day, we're all connected to the vine; what matters is our connection. These differences are artificially created to fool us.

Then I ask myself: Where did I come from? What am I supposed to be doing? My soul came from elsewhere; I'm sure of that and intend to return there. I don't remember where I came from, but I know I must have originated in some other realm, a tavern perhaps. The day will come when I fly off.

Whoever is now speaking through my voice? Who speaks within my mouth? What does a soul look like when it cannot stop asking these questions? If I could taste the answer, I would break out of this prison for drunks. I didn't come here on my own; I can't leave that way. Whoever brought me here must take me home.

This is beautiful and echoes Plato's allegory of the cave. We are all in a prison for drunks, blind from our true reality. When we return to the Monad and Master, we will see the truth for ourselves. Another prophet, Friedrich Nietzsche, was one of the three great German philosophers—Emanuel Kant, Friedrich Hegel, and Friedrich Nietzsche wrote about Zoroaster's words, taking long walks in the mountains where he felt seized by a force compelling him to speak as Zoroaster.

Reading what Nietzsche writes, you'll see it is similar to what Zoroaster himself promoted. Nietzsche speaks from a modern, contemporary lens but his message aligns with Zoroaster’s teachings.
